source.title: Serial dependence in visual perception: A meta-analysis and review

confidence_rationale: A rigorous meta-analysis establishing that perception is systematically biased toward the recent past (serial dependence), tuned by time, space, feature-similarity, and attention. For MECH-456 this is genuinely two-directional: it is strong evidence for the STABILITY COUNTERWEIGHT that a rebinding mechanism must overcome, and therefore for the DESIGN choice of a threshold (rebind only when a competitor decisively overtakes, not on every fluctuation) rather than free chatter. But on its own face serial dependence is a persistence/hysteresis phenomenon -- the force OPPOSING rebinding -- so it does not directly support that rebinding occurs, only that if it does it must clear a hysteresis band. Marked mixed for that reason.
failure_signatures: Serial dependence is, at face value, evidence for perceptual STICKINESS -- the opposite of rebinding. A skeptic could read it as showing the system resists switching, i.e. as pressure AGAINST MECH-456's re-bind-on-overtake dynamic rather than for it.

The phenomenon is characterised on low-level continuous features (orientation, numerosity, face identity) in human psychophysics, not on discrete self<->world-configuration bindings; the 'threshold/hysteresis' transfer is a design analogy, not a measured property of any binder.
Meta-analysis of many small-N studies with heterogeneous paradigms; individual differences are large, so the magnitude of the hysteresis a binder should emulate is not pinned down.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Serial dependence is a robust, systematic bias in which current perception, decision, and memory of a feature or object are attracted toward what was seen in the recent past. The meta-analysis shows it is defined by four tunings -- it decays over time (temporal), depends on relative spatial location (spatial), occurs only between similar features/objects (feature), and is modulated by attention -- constituting a general mechanism that smooths perception into an 'illusory stability' across time.
mapping.ree_translation: Serial dependence is the biological name for the STABILITY COUNTERWEIGHT in MECH-456's design. The claim explicitly frames rebinding against 'the stability counterweight rebinding must overcome, motivating a threshold rather than chatter.' Manassi/Murai/Whitney supply the empirical warrant for that counterweight: perception carries an online hysteresis toward the recent past. A well-formed rebinding rule therefore should NOT flip the self<->world-config binding on every transient fluctuation; it should require a competitor to overtake decisively -- exactly the threshold/hysteresis band MECH-456 posits, and the feature-tuning result ('only between similar objects') even predicts that competition is scored between comparable configurations.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is the counterweight, not the switch -- it evidences the FORCE OPPOSING rebinding and the NEED for a threshold, not that rebinding happens. It is measured on low-level continuous visual features in humans, not on discrete latent bindings; the mapping onto a binder's rebind threshold is an architectural analogy. Do not read it as direct support that REE's binder re-binds.
mapping.source_context: Meta-analysis and review of human visual psychophysics across orientation, face, and numerosity perception.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality very high (quantitative meta-analysis, canonical authors). Mapping fidelity deliberately moderate-low (0.5): it grounds the DESIGN necessity of a rebinding threshold but is the opposing-force phenomenon, hence evidence_direction=mixed. Transfer risk moderate: human low-level feature psychophysics -> latent-binding threshold.
